title: Failures too
hook: Muslim history includes cruelty and injustice, and the tradition itself criticizes it

segments.voice: Yesterday, mercy in power: the leniency the Qur'an praised in the Prophet, and the shepherd in every household. Your line was mercy is remembered. Where did you answer one notch gentler? Day one thousand fifty-two.

Who wrote down the day of Karbala? Not an enemy of Islam. Muslim historians did, al-Tabari among them, and they set down, in plain detail, an army of a Muslim ruler killing the Prophet's own grandson and many of his family. Names, speeches, who struck whom. They didn't bury it. They copied it, taught it, and argued over it. That's worth sitting with. This path has told a lot of history this year with admiration. Today it turns the other way, and asks what the tradition does with its own worst days. Today: failures too.
screen: `WHO WROTE DOWN KARBALA?` → `MUSLIM HISTORIANS DID.` → `THEY DIDN'T BURY IT.`

segments.voice: There were cruel rulers. Unjust wars. Prisoners mistreated, scholars jailed, the poor taxed to pay for palaces. Muslim history holds all of that, the way every long human history does. The surprising part is where the sharpest criticism came from: inside. First, the standard. The Qur'an asks believers to tell the truth even when it costs their own side. In Pickthall's translation: "O ye who believe! Be ye staunch in justice, witnesses for Allah, even though it be against yourselves or (your) parents or (your) kindred." Against yourselves. That includes your own dynasty and your own history. Second, the voice. A hadith in the Sunan of Abu Dawud calls a word of justice spoken before an unjust ruler the best kind of striving. Third, the people who paid for it. The scholar Ahmad ibn Hanbal was imprisoned and beaten under the caliph's officials for refusing to say what the court required. Hasan al-Basri, whom we met earlier, admonished the governors of his day. Their students kept their names and honored them; the officials who did the beating are mostly footnotes. Fourth, the mirror. In the Qur'an, Adam and his wife did wrong in the garden, and their answer is the model of an honest believer, in Pickthall's words: "Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves." No excuses, no blaming the other. That's the lesson history leaves for a single life: the faith is strong enough to name its failures, and so is a person.
screen: `CRUELTY AND INJUSTICE HAPPENED.` · `STAUNCH IN JUSTICE, EVEN AGAINST YOURSELVES.` · `A WORD OF JUSTICE BEFORE A TYRANT.` · `OUR LORD, WE HAVE WRONGED OURSELVES.`

segments.voice: The practice: admit one failure. Settle, and breathe. Let one thing come up that you got wrong, recently or long ago. Not the worst thing you've ever done. Just one real one. A sharp word. A promise dropped. A time you took the easy side. Look at it straight, the way those historians looked at Karbala, without dressing it up and without beating yourself with it. Say it to yourself in one plain sentence: I did this. If you pray, you can say the words of Adam and his wife: our Lord, we have wronged ourselves. The bell holds the time.
Failures too. Muslim history holds cruelty and injustice, and the tradition's own scholars and historians named them. Today's word.
Your line: honesty is faith. Today, if the failure you named touched someone, tell them so, in one plain sentence. Day one thousand fifty-two.

howItsDone: Muslims seek forgiveness (istighfar) from God daily, and the tradition teaches that wronging another person also requires putting it right with that person.

fork.setup: you're a scholar summoned to court. the caliph's officials want you to say something you believe is false. refusing means prison. what do you do?
options: say it; the ruler's word settles it.
say it now and take it back once you're free.
fork.reveal: Ahmad ibn Hanbal refused, and was imprisoned and beaten. his students remembered him, not the officials.

original.note: Arabic: wrongdoing, injustice. the same root is in "we have wronged ourselves" (7:23).

trapdoor: what you thought: a faith's history is told by its admirers, so its failures get left out.
what it means: Muslim history holds cruelty and injustice, and the tradition's own voices named it.
what a scholar hears: Qur'an 4:135 demands witness against yourselves; al-Tabari records Karbala; Ahmad ibn Hanbal's refusal under the caliph's officials is honored by his students.

notes: Pickthall 4:135 matches wording used elsewhere on this path; 7:23 fragment quoted from memory. Confirm both.
Abu Dawud 4344 paraphrased as 'among the best kinds of striving'; confirm number and wording.
Ahmad ibn Hanbal in the Mihna (imprisoned and flogged for refusing the doctrine of the created Qur'an) is described without dates or caliphs' names; the doctrine is not named. Confirm framing.
'Their students kept their names and made them heroes, not the officials' is an interpretive line; Keeper may soften.
The opening list of failures is general (cruel rulers, unjust wars, prisoners, taxes) with no specific claims.
Original note says ẓulm shares a root with ẓalamnā in 7:23; confirm.
Editor: cut the unsourced superlative 'one of the great imams' and 'the Qur'an's first humans' (not stated in 7:23).

Audit: Abu Dawud 4344 reads 'the best jihad is a word of justice before a tyrannical ruler'; the script's 'among the best kinds' misquoted it and now follows the hadith. 'Their students... not the officials who beat them' implied Hasan al-Basri was beaten too; reworded so only Ibn Hanbal is beaten, and Hasan 'admonished the governors of his day'. Hook's 'by a river they weren't allowed to drink from' cut: it repeated day 1047's Karbala thirst image.
